title: Fabrication of albumin nanoparticles for controlled lenalidomide delivery: enhanced stability and anticancer potential in multiple myeloma
content: Lenalidomide (LN) is an immunomodulatory drug (IMiD) whose main mechanism centres on reprogramming a cereblon-based E3 ubiquitin ligase complex to degrade specific proteins that drive tumour survival and immune dysfunction. LN was developed as a second-generation thalidomide analogue to improve potency and reduce neurotoxicity. However, dose-limiting toxicity including neutropenia, thrombocytopenia (myelosuppression), and an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, have hurdled its clinical application. LN resistance is a major clinical drawback because patients often relapse or become refractory after an initial response. To overcome these challenges, we synthesised lenalidomide bovine serum albumin nanoparticles (BSA–LN-NPs) for albumin-mediated cancer therapy and overcome the dose-limiting toxicity. The synthesised BSA–LN-NPs exhibited a uniform spherical morphology with an average hydrodynamic diameter (Z-average, Dh) of 203 ± 1.3 nm, zeta potential of −25.9 ± 1.9 mV, and a polydispersity index of 0.13 ± 0.02. FTIR provided evidence of LN incorporation into the BSA nanoparticle matrix. XRD analysis revealed complete amorphisation of LN, indicating a transition from its crystalline state to an amorphous form within the BSA–LN-NPs. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) revealed only a single endotherm for BSA–LN-NPs at 240.6 °C, with neither the characteristic of BSA denaturation peaks nor the LN melting point elucidating proper encapsulation and dispersion of LN in the nanoparticle matrix. Further differential thermogravimetry (DTG) complemented and validated the DSC findings. Upon reconstitution, the lyophilised BSA–LN-NPs showed no significant changes in particle size, zeta potential, PDI, or encapsulation efficiency, maintaining a re-dispersibility index (RDI) of 1, indicating complete re-dispersibility and preserved colloidal integrity. In vitro release kinetics demonstrated sustained drug release for up to 4 days. BSA–LN-NPs displayed higher potent cytotoxicity in the KMS-11 cell line compared to free LN. Serum stability test carried out in 10% FBS over 48 h revealed no significant change in Dh, indicating good colloidal stability of the NPs. Overall, BSA–LN-NPs offer a promising strategy for the sustained delivery of LN, with comparable to or greater cytotoxicity in KMS-11 cells than that of free LN.
